64.title: Remember me (Luke 23:32–43)
64.hook: a dying thief asks to be remembered and is promised paradise today
64.howItsDone: Catholics hear the good thief's words in the Passion on Good Friday, and many ask Saint Dismas to pray for the dying and for people in prison.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before Pilate: are you a king, and the washed hands. Your line was what is truth. Did you stay with a hard question a minute longer? Day sixty-four. A new week: the cross and the morning.

A hill outside the city walls, called the place of the skull. Calvary, in the old Latin. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle, and two criminals, one on each side. The crowd watches. Soldiers throw dice for his clothes. And the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross, in the Douay-Rheims, is this: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Then the men beside him start talking. One of them joins the mocking: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us. And the other one, who has nothing left, no time, no chance to make anything right, turns his head and says something nobody expects. Today: the shortest conversation in the Gospels.
screen: `THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.` → `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` → `TWO MEN, TWO VERY DIFFERENT WORDS.`

segments.voice: The second man tells the first to stop. We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he says to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." That's all. No speech. No list of what he did. Just remember me. And Jesus answers: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Paradise is a Persian word that came into Greek. It first meant a walled garden, the kind a king kept. Jewish writers used it for the garden of Eden, and then for the place where God keeps the righteous. So a man dying on a cross is promised a garden, and not someday. This day. The Gospel never gives his name. Later Christian writings called him Dismas, and Catholics know him as the good thief, a saint, and pray to him for the dying and for prisoners. Here's why Catholics love him so much. As far as anyone knows, he was never baptized. He never had time to make amends. He had one honest sentence in him, at the very end, and it was enough. The Church uses this story to say that mercy can reach anyone, right up to the last breath. One more scholar's detail. The oldest Greek manuscripts had almost no punctuation, so people have argued over where the comma goes: I say to you today, or, today you will be with me. The Church has read it the way the Douay-Rheims prints it: this day.
screen: `LORD, REMEMBER ME.` · `PARADISE: A WALLED GARDEN.` · `THE GOOD THIEF, DISMAS.` · `ONE HONEST SENTENCE AT THE END.` · then, large: `THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME IN PARADISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to be remembered, simply. Settle and breathe. No long list, no explaining yourself. Just notice what it's like to want to be remembered, by someone you love, or by God. Let the wanting be there without dressing it up. If you pray, you can use the thief's own words, slowly, a few times: Lord, remember me. If you don't, you can just hold the wish quietly and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Remember me. What a dying thief asked for, with nothing to offer, and the answer he got: today. Today's word.
Your line: this day in paradise. Today, remember someone who might feel forgotten, and tell them so, in one plain sentence. Day sixty-four.

65.title: His mother stood (John 19:25–27)
65.hook: Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple as his mother
65.howItsDone: Catholics sing or pray the Stabat Mater during the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, and honor Mary as Mother of the Church on the Monday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember me: a dying thief asked for one thing and was promised a garden. Your line was this day in paradise. Who did you remember out loud? Day sixty-five.

Think about the worst hospital waiting room you've ever sat in. Nothing to do. Nothing to fix. You stay because leaving is unthinkable. Now go back to the hill. Most of the men who followed Jesus have scattered. But John's Gospel slows down and names who is still there, standing by the cross: his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. And one disciple, the one the Gospel only ever calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. They can't stop it. They can't even get close enough to wipe his face. They stand. Today's word is three words from that verse.
screen: `NOTHING TO FIX. YOU STAY.` → `FOUR WOMEN AND ONE DISCIPLE.` → `THEY STAND.`

segments.voice: Then Jesus, who can barely breathe, spends some of his last words on this. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, behold thy son." And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." And John adds: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman sounds cold to us. It isn't. It's the same word he used for her at the wedding at Cana, a word of respect, and some readers hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis. There are two ways to hear this moment, and Catholics hold both. The first is simple and human. A dying son makes sure his widowed mother will have a home. That alone is worth sitting with. The second is bigger. The Gospel never names the beloved disciple. Tradition says it was John, but leaving him unnamed lets every disciple stand in his place. So Catholics read it as Jesus giving his mother to all of us, and they call Mary the Mother of the Church. Pope Paul VI gave her that title during the Second Vatican Council. Then there's the word stood. In the Latin Bible it's stabat, and a medieval hymn opens with it: Stabat Mater, the mother stood. It's sung on Good Friday and during the Stations of the Cross. She didn't faint. She didn't leave. She stood.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand beside someone who is suffering. Settle and breathe. Bring one person to mind who is going through something you can't fix. Picture yourself not fixing it. Just standing near them, the way Mary stood. Notice how hard it is to do nothing but stay. Then think of one small way to be there this week: a visit, a call, sitting with them in silence. If you pray, you can ask Mary to stand with them too. The bell holds the time.
His mother stood. Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple, and, Catholics say, to all of us. Today's word.
Your line: behold thy mother. Today, look after someone else's mother, or someone who mothered you, in one small, practical way. Day sixty-five.

66.title: It is finished (Luke 23:44–56)
66.hook: darkness, the veil torn, into thy hands, and a borrowed tomb
66.howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics celebrate no Mass; they gather for the Passion, prayers, the veneration of the cross and communion from hosts consecrated the night before, and many pray night prayer with the words into your hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his mother stood at the foot of the cross, and he gave her to his friend. Your line was behold thy mother. Who did you look after? Day sixty-six. Today is the hardest hour of the story.

Walk into a Catholic church on Good Friday afternoon and it feels wrong on purpose. The tabernacle stands open and empty. The altar is stripped bare: no cloth, no candles, no flowers. There's no Mass. It's the one day of the year the Church doesn't celebrate one. The priest walks in and lies face down on the floor in silence. Then the Passion is read aloud, the whole story, and at one moment everyone in the church kneels, and nobody says a word for a while. Today is that moment, the way Luke tells it.
screen: `A STRIPPED ALTAR.` → `NO MASS, ONE DAY A YEAR.` → `EVERYONE KNEELS.`

segments.voice: It's about noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until three in the afternoon. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst." The veil was the great curtain in the temple that hid the holiest place, where only the high priest went, once a year. Christians have read its tearing as the way to God being opened. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Those words aren't new. They're from a psalm, a prayer every faithful Jew would have known, and he dies praying it. Today's title, it is finished, comes from John's Gospel, where the Douay-Rheims renders it "It is consummated." In Greek it's one word, used for a job completed or a debt paid in full. Two Gospels, two last words, and the Church keeps both. Then small, human things happen. A Roman centurion who has watched it all says: "Indeed this was a just man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. A council member named Joseph, from a town called Arimathea, who had not agreed with the others, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut from rock where no one had ever been laid. The women from Galilee follow to see where. They go home, prepare spices, and rest on the Sabbath, as the law asked. And every night, in the Church's night prayer, Catholics say his last words again: into your hands.
screen: `DARKNESS, AND THE VEIL TORN.` · `A PSALM ON HIS LIPS.` · `IT IS CONSUMMATED: PAID IN FULL.` · `A CENTURION, A TOMB, THE WOMEN.` · then, large: `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: silence. Settle and breathe. There's nothing to picture today and nothing to do. Just let it be quiet, the way the church goes quiet when everyone kneels. If thoughts come, let them go by. If you pray, you can say his words once, at the start, and then say nothing more: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. Then stay in the quiet until the bell. The bell holds the time.
It is finished. In Greek, one word for a finished task or a debt paid in full, and in Luke, a psalm prayed with the last breath. Today's word.
Your line: into thy hands. Tonight, before you sleep, hand the day over, the good and the unfinished, in whatever words you have. Day sixty-six.

67.title: Holy Saturday
67.hook: the day of silence; the Church says he went down to free the dead (CCC 632–635)
67.carry: god is in the silence too
67.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday Catholic churches celebrate no Mass during the day; the tabernacle stays empty, and the Church waits in prayer until the Easter Vigil after nightfall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, it is finished: darkness, the veil torn, a psalm on his lips, and a tomb cut from rock. Your line was into thy hands. Did you hand the day over last night? Day sixty-seven.

Everyone knows a day in between. The day after the phone call and before the funeral. The day you're waiting for a test result. Nothing happens, and it's the heaviest day of the week. The Gospels give the Saturday after the cross exactly one line. Luke says the women rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment. That's it. No words from Jesus. No miracles. A sealed tomb, and people sitting at home with spices they can't use yet. The Church keeps that day on purpose. On Holy Saturday there's no Mass during the day. The tabernacle is still empty. Catholics wait. Today is the silent day.
screen: `THE DAY IN BETWEEN.` → `ONE LINE IN THE GOSPELS.` → `THE CHURCH WAITS.`

segments.voice: But the Church doesn't say nothing happened. It says something happened where no one could see. In the old Apostles' Creed, Catholics say: "He descended into hell." That word trips people up. Here it doesn't mean the place of the damned. The Catechism explains it means the realm of all the dead, what the Hebrew Bible calls Sheol. Jesus really died, the Church says, so he went where the dead go. And he didn't go to be stuck there. He went to open it, to bring out the just who had died before him, all the way back to Adam and Eve. The First Letter of Peter says he went and preached to the spirits in prison. Eastern Christians paint it. Their Easter icon doesn't show an empty tomb. It shows Christ standing on broken doors, the locks scattered, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their graves by the wrists. And an ancient sermon for this day, read by Catholics in the Church's morning prayers on Holy Saturday, begins by saying there is a great silence on the earth, because the King is asleep. Then it follows him down, to go looking for Adam. So on the quietest day of the year, the Church says God was at work in the deepest place. Nobody saw it. It didn't make a sound. That's the point: silence isn't the same as absence.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep quiet, and don't fill it. Settle and breathe. Put the phone face down, out of reach. Let whatever is unfinished in your life stay unfinished for two minutes. You don't have to understand it or fix it. Just wait, the way the women waited with their spices. If you pray, you can simply stay in God's presence without words. If you don't, you can notice what silence actually sounds like. The bell holds the time.
Holy Saturday. The silent day between the cross and the morning, when the Church says he went down to free the dead. Today's word.
Your line: god is in the silence too. Today, keep one hour of quiet: no music, no podcast, no scrolling. Notice what comes up. Day sixty-seven.

68.title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:1–18)
68.hook: she thinks he's the gardener until he says her name
68.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of Mary Magdalene at the tomb on Easter Sunday morning, and keep her feast on 22 July as the apostle to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, the silent day, when the Church says he went down to free the dead. Your line was god is in the silence too. What came up in your hour of quiet? Day sixty-eight. It's morning.

You're in a crowded place, an airport, a stadium, a busy store, and out of all that noise someone says your name. Not shouts it. Just says it, the way only people who know you say it. And your head turns before you've decided to turn it. Hold on to that. Early on the first day of the week, while it's still dark, Mary Magdalene walks to the tomb. The stone has been rolled away. The body is gone. She runs for Peter, they come and look and go home, and she stays outside the tomb, crying. Today: what happens to the one who stayed.
screen: `YOUR NAME, ACROSS A CROWD.` → `STILL DARK. THE STONE MOVED.` → `SHE STAYS, CRYING.`

segments.voice: She bends to look into the tomb and sees two angels, who ask why she's weeping. They've taken my Lord away, she says, and I don't know where they've laid him. She turns around, and there's a man standing there. In the Douay-Rheims he asks: "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener. Sir, she says, if you've moved him, tell me where, and I'll take him. And then he says one word. "Mary." That's all. Not a proof. Not a speech. Her name. And she knows him. She turns and says: "Rabboni," which John explains means Master, my teacher. Notice the Gospel's honesty. She doesn't recognize the risen Jesus by his face. She knows him by the way he says her name. Then he sends her. Go to my brothers, he says, and tell them. And she goes to the disciples and says: "I have seen the Lord." She is the first witness of the resurrection in John's Gospel, sent to tell the ones who will tell everyone else. That's why the Church has long called her the apostle to the apostles, and in 2016 Pope Francis raised her day, 22 July, to a feast, like the apostles' own. One more thing to clear up. For centuries people called her a repentant prostitute. The Gospels never say that. It came from later preaching that blended her with other women in the Gospels, and the Church's calendar separated them again in 1969.

Christians believe God knows each person by name, like that. If you pray, you can sit quietly and imagine your name said with that kind of love. The bell holds the time.

69.title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
69.hook: two sad friends walk seven miles with a stranger and know him in the breaking of bread
69.howItsDone: Catholics often hear the Emmaus story during the Easter season, and many see in it the two parts of every Mass: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene in the garden: she took him for the gardener until he said her name. Your line was he says your name. Whose name did you say like it mattered? Day sixty-nine.

Same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away. One is named Cleophas. The other, Luke never names. They're going over it again and again, the way you do after a funeral, on the long drive home. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop. Their faces fall. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn't heard? And then the saddest words in the chapter: we had hoped he was the one. Had hoped. Past tense. Today: the longest walk of Easter day.
screen: `SEVEN MILES, WALKING HOME.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `WE HAD HOPED.`

segments.voice: The stranger is Jesus, but Luke says their eyes were held so they didn't know him. And he doesn't reveal himself. He walks with them and opens the Scriptures, from Moses through all the prophets, showing how the Messiah had to suffer and so enter his glory. Seven miles of Bible study. At the village he acts as if he's going further. And they beg him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." He goes in. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them. The same four movements as the Last Supper. And their eyes are opened, they know him, and he vanishes. Then they turn to each other: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" It's dark, and they walk the seven miles back anyway, to tell the others how they knew him "in the breaking of bread." Catholics see the shape of every Mass in this road. First the Word: the Scriptures read and opened. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Two parts, the same order Luke tells it. And notice where he's recognized. Not in the explaining, as good as it was. In the bread. Pope John Paul II named a letter on the Eucharist after the disciples' plea, stay with us, Lord.

Think of one question you could ask them this week, and then just listen. If you pray, you can ask to be good company on someone's road. The bell holds the time.

70.title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
70.hook: he wanted to touch the wounds, and then said my Lord and my God
70.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Thomas every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some quietly say 'my Lord and my God' when the host is raised at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Emmaus: seven miles with a stranger, and bread broken at the end. Your line was was not our heart burning. What warmed you yesterday that you only noticed later? Day seventy.

Somebody in every group chat is the one who says, pics or it didn't happen. That's Thomas. On Easter night the risen Jesus comes to the disciples behind locked doors, and Thomas isn't there. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he doesn't believe a word. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." Not just see. Touch. For two thousand years he's been called doubting Thomas. Today: what actually happened eight days later.
screen: `PICS OR IT DIDN'T HAPPEN.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.` → `I WILL NOT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: First, who Thomas was. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back toward Jerusalem, where people had tried to stone him, it's Thomas who says: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." He's not a coward. He's blunt, and loyal, and he won't pretend. Eight days after Easter, they're together again, and this time Thomas is there. The doors are shut. Jesus stands in the middle and says, "Peace be to you." Then he turns to Thomas and offers him exactly what he asked for: put in your finger, see my hands, bring your hand, put it into my side, "and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't scold him for asking. He shows him the wounds. And here's the surprise: the Gospel never says Thomas touched them. What it gives us is his answer: "My Lord, and my God." Nobody in any of the Gospels says anything bigger about who Jesus is. The doubter makes the fullest confession of faith. Then Jesus adds a line for everyone after: "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." That means the listener, too. Catholics hear this Gospel every year on the Sunday after Easter. And there's an old Catholic custom: when the priest lifts the host at Mass, some people whisper Thomas's words. My Lord and my God. Tradition says Thomas later carried the faith all the way to India, and Christians there still call themselves Saint Thomas Christians. So that was the week: remember me, his mother stood, it is finished, Holy Saturday, the garden, Emmaus, and Thomas.
